notes: Rana tigrina (tiger frog / Indian bullfrog): the model amphibian for NEB; ~5–8 cm long; found in ponds, streams, and wet grasslands.
Habit and habitat: semi-aquatic; lives near water but spends most of the day on land; returns to water to breed; buries in moist soil in dry season.

External features: moist, glandular, scaleless skin (mucus + colour glands); head with eyes, tympanum (eardrum), nostrils; distinct neck, trunk; 4-digit forelimbs, 5-digit webbed hindlimbs; nictitating membrane (third eyelid); tail absent in adults (present in tadpole).
Skin: mucus glands (keep skin moist for cutaneous respiration) and granular/colour (poison) glands; highly permeable to water and gases.
Body plan: vertebrate (internal skeleton), amphibian (dual life); metamorphosis from tadpole (gills + tail) to frog (lungs, no tail).
Taxonomy: Animalia > Chordata > Vertebrata > Amphibia > Anura > Rana.
NEB focus: general features, habit and habitat, and external anatomy of Rana tigrina as the entry topic for frog anatomy.
Importance: pest control (eats insects), water-quality bio-indicator, food in some regions; sensitive to environmental change.
Key adaptation summary: moist skin, webbed feet, tympanum, nictitating membrane, sticky pads — all for an amphibious (land + water) life.
confusion: Frogs are amphibians (cold-blooded, moist skin, larval gills), NOT reptiles (dry scaly skin, lungs only).
Adult frogs have NO tail; the tadpole larva has a tail (metamorphosis removes it).
The forelimbs have 4 digits and the hindlimbs have 5 webbed digits — a key exam detail.
The tympanum is the external eardrum; the nictitating membrane is a transparent third eyelid for underwater vision.
Frogs breathe through lungs, moist skin (cutaneous), and the buccal cavity; tadpoles use gills.
Rana tigrina lives in moist habitats; its permeable skin makes it a sensitive bio-indicator of water pollution.

universalFacts: Rana tigrina (the "tiger frog") is one of the largest common freshwater frogs in South Asia.
The frog skin is so permeable that it can absorb both water and pollutants — the basis of its bio-indicator role.
The tadpole-to-frog metamorphosis takes 2–3 months in most species.
Frogs are ectothermic (cold-blooded); body temperature changes with the environment.
examples: Habitat: a frog sitting on a pond bank by day, entering water at night to feed and breed.
External: webbed hind feet (swimming), sticky pads on forefeet (climbing), tympanum (hearing), nictitating membrane (eye protection).
Metamorphosis: tadpole (tail + gills) → froglet → adult frog (lungs, no tail).
Bio-indicator: frogs die off in polluted ponds, warning of water-quality decline.
